title: ITD 256 Midterm Review
description: Matches the exam structure: theory & SQL, ERD completion, and normalization/dependency sets.

questions.question: In the file/database terminology hierarchy, what is a 'field' also known as?
questions.explanation: A field is a character or group of characters with specific meaning, also known as an attribute.

questions.question: A logically connected set of fields that describes a person, place, or thing is called a:
questions.explanation: A record is a logically connected set of one or more fields describing a person, place, or thing (also called an entity instance).

questions.question: Match each file/database term to its definition.

pairs.right: Raw facts with little meaning until organized
Character(s) with specific meaning; also called an attribute
Set of related fields describing a person, place, or thing
Collection of related records; also called an entity

questions.explanation: This mirrors Table 1.2's basic file terminology: data, field, record, and table build on one another.

questions.question: Which type of data exists in its original, raw state with no formatting applied?
questions.explanation: Unstructured data exists in its original (raw) state, before any structure/formatting has been applied. Semistructured data (e.g. XML) is only partially processed.

questions.question: A database created and maintained via a cloud service, with defined performance measures, is classified (by location) as a:
questions.explanation: Classification by location includes centralized, distributed, and cloud databases; a cloud database is created and maintained with cloud services.

questions.question: When a file's structure can be changed without requiring every program that accesses it to also be modified, this describes:
questions.explanation: Structural independence means access to a file doesn't depend on its own structure; structural dependence means programs must be modified whenever the file structure changes.

questions.question: In discussions of data independence, the way data is represented to an application or user is the ______ format, while how it's actually stored on hardware is the physical format (and should be hidden from the user).
questions.explanation: Logical format is the representation to the application/user; physical format is the actual storage on hardware.

questions.question: A customer's address is stored separately in both a Billing table and a Shipping table. Updating it in only one place leaves the two out of sync. This scenario illustrates:
options: Data redundancy leading to an update anomaly
questions.explanation: Unnecessarily storing the same data in different places is data redundancy; when required changes aren't made everywhere consistently, that's an update anomaly.

questions.question: Which DBMS function is responsible for storing definitions of data elements and their relationships?
questions.explanation: Data dictionary management stores the definitions of data elements and their relationships in the data dictionary.

questions.question: A restriction placed on data to help ensure data integrity is called a ______ — one of the four basic data model building blocks, along with entity, attribute, and relationship.
questions.explanation: Entity, attribute, relationship, and constraint are the four basic building blocks of a data model.

questions.question: When translating business rules into a data model, the relationships you identify between entities are always bidirectional.
questions.explanation: Relationships are always bidirectional — you have to ask how many instances of B relate to one instance of A, and vice versa.

questions.question: The older ERD notation style that represents entities as rectangles and relationships as diamonds is called ______ notation (as opposed to the Crow's Foot notation used on this course's ERDs).
questions.explanation: Chen notation uses diamond shapes for relationships; this course primarily uses Crow's Foot notation instead.

questions.question: In the relational model, a 'relation' is another name for a:
questions.explanation: A relation is a matrix of intersecting rows and columns — in other words, a table or entity.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a relational database management system (RDBMS)?
options: It replaces SQL with a graphical query builder
It makes the relational model easier to understand and implement, hiding its complexities from the user
It only supports one table per database
It stores data exclusively in XML format
questions.explanation: An RDBMS performs the functions of hierarchical/network DBMSs but makes the relational model easier to use by hiding its complexities.

questions.question: A natural key is best described as:
options: An artificially made-up identifier such as an auto-number
A real-world identifier that already uniquely identifies real-world objects
A key composed of multiple attributes
A key used strictly for data retrieval
questions.explanation: A natural key (or natural identifier) is a real-world identifier already familiar to end users that uniquely identifies real-world objects.

questions.question: A surrogate primary key is especially useful when:
options: There's an obvious short natural key available
The primary key would otherwise be composite with multiple data types, or too long to be usable
The table has no foreign keys
The table only has one row
questions.explanation: Surrogate keys are useful when no natural key is suitable, when the primary key would be composite with multiple data types, or when it would be too long to be usable.

questions.question: A candidate key is defined as:
options: A foreign key in another table
questions.explanation: A candidate key is a minimal superkey — a superkey with no unnecessary attributes.

questions.question: A key used strictly for data retrieval purposes, rather than to enforce uniqueness or link tables, is called a ______ key.
questions.explanation: A secondary key is used strictly for data retrieval purposes (e.g. searching by last name), unlike a primary or foreign key.

questions.question: Entity integrity requires that:
options: Every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value
All primary key values are unique, and no part of the primary key can be null
Every table must have at least one foreign key
All attributes must allow null values
questions.explanation: Entity integrity: every row has a unique identity — all primary key entries are unique and no part of the primary key is null.

questions.question: ______ integrity requires that every foreign key value be either null or match an existing primary key value in the related table.
questions.explanation: Referential integrity governs the validity of foreign key references between tables.

questions.question: The complete logical view of a database — a full description of every table, relationship, and constraint in it — is called the database ______.
questions.explanation: The database schema is the complete logical view of the database; a relational schema refers to this for an individual table.

questions.question: In a relational database, the order of rows and columns does not matter to the DBMS.
questions.explanation: One of the defining characteristics of a relational table is that row/column order is irrelevant to the DBMS.

questions.question: A foreign key value must always match an existing primary key value in the related table and can never be null.
questions.explanation: Referential integrity allows a foreign key to be either null or a value matching an existing primary key — it doesn't have to match.

questions.question: Match each SELECT clause to what it does.

pairs.right: Specifies the attributes/columns to be returned
Specifies the table(s) data is retrieved from
Filters individual rows based on given criteria
Groups rows into collections sharing the same value(s)
Filters the groups formed by GROUP BY
Sorts the final result rows ascending or descending

questions.explanation: A full SELECT statement is built in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.

questions.question: Match each SQL command category to what it's used for.

pairs.right: Defines database structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP)
Manipulates data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT)
Controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK)
Controls data access permissions

questions.explanation: SQL functions fall into four categories: DDL, DML, TCL, and DCL.

questions.question: Which SQL command permanently deletes an entire database, including all of its tables?
questions.explanation: DROP DATABASE permanently deletes the entire database, including all tables. DROP TABLE only removes a single table.

questions.question: Inside a CREATE TABLE statement, which keyword ensures a column can never contain duplicate values?
questions.explanation: UNIQUE ensures a column has no duplicate values. NOT NULL only prevents nulls; CHECK validates data against a condition; DEFAULT supplies a value when none is given.

questions.question: Two tables share no identically-named columns, so you need to join them on a condition like film.language_id = language.language_id. Which join syntax fits?
options: A join isn't possible without matching column names
questions.explanation: JOIN ... ON lets you express a join condition explicitly, which is required when the tables have no common attribute name to rely on.

questions.question: SQL's NATURAL JOIN automatically matches columns with identical names and compatible data types, without needing an ON or USING clause.
questions.explanation: NATURAL JOIN determines common attributes itself by finding identically-named, compatible-type columns.

questions.question: An EMPLOYEE table has a MANAGER_ID column that references another employee's own EMP_ID in that same table. Joining EMPLOYEE to itself to pair each employee with their manager is an example of a:
questions.explanation: A recursive join is unary — it joins a table to itself. All other join types are binary (between two different tables).

questions.question: The HAVING clause filters individual rows before they are grouped by GROUP BY.
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups that GROUP BY already formed.

questions.question: The SQL clause used to filter groups after GROUP BY is called ______.
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups formed by GROUP BY, based on aggregate conditions.

questions.question: Match each SQL special operator to what it does.

pairs.right: Tests whether a value falls within a range, inclusive of both endpoints
Tests whether a value matches any value in a given list
Matches a value against a text pattern using wildcards
Tests whether a value is missing/absent

questions.explanation: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, and IS NULL/NOT NULL are the special comparison operators covered alongside AND/OR/NOT.

questions.question: In a SQL LIKE pattern such as '%HOTEL%', the % symbol is a wildcard that matches ______ (how many characters?).
questions.explanation: % matches any sequence of zero or more characters; the underscore _ wildcard matches exactly one character.

questions.question: Match each aggregate function to what it computes.

pairs.right: The number of rows (or non-null values) in a set
The smallest / largest value in a set
The total of all values in a set
The mean of all values in a set

questions.explanation: Aggregate functions take a collection of rows and reduce them to a single summary row.

questions.question: The acronym CRUD stands for Create, Read, ______, and Delete.
questions.explanation: CRUD maps to INSERT (Create), SELECT (Read), UPDATE, and DELETE.

questions.question: It's safe to run an UPDATE or DELETE statement without a WHERE clause, since SQL will always ask for confirmation before applying it to every row.
questions.explanation: SQL does not confirm before acting — an UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE clause immediately applies to every row in the table. Always use WHERE to limit the damage.

questions.question: Write a query to select all columns from the film table.
rubric: Used SELECT * to return every column
Named the correct table: film
questions.explanation: SELECT * returns every column; no WHERE clause means every row too.

questions.question: Write a query to select the title and rental_rate columns from film, but only for rows where rental_rate is greater than 4.
rubric: Selected exactly the title and rental_rate columns
Named the correct table: film
WHERE condition correctly filters rental_rate > 4
questions.explanation: SELECT names the columns you want; WHERE restricts which rows qualify.

questions.question:
Complete this query to count how many customers are in the customer table:

SELECT ____ FROM customer;
rubric: Used COUNT(*) (or an equivalent aggregate) to count rows
Named the correct table: customer
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) is an aggregate function that reduces all matching rows to a single count.

questions.question: Write a query using DISTINCT to list the unique rating values from the film table.
rubric: Used SELECT DISTINCT
Selected the correct column: rating
Named the correct table: film
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate values so each rating appears only once.

questions.question: Write a query that joins film, film_category (using film_id), and category (using category_id) to list the titles of films where category.name = 'Comedy'.
questions.modelAnswer:
SELECT title
FROM film
INNER JOIN film_category USING (film_id)
INNER JOIN category USING (category_id)
WHERE category.name = 'Comedy';
rubric: Selected the title column
Joined film to film_category on film_id
Joined film_category to category on category_id
WHERE condition correctly filters category.name = 'Comedy'
questions.explanation: Chaining two INNER JOIN ... USING clauses links all three tables through their shared key columns.

questions.question: Write a query to select rental_id, rental_date, inventory_id, and customer_id from the rental table, where rental_date is between '2005-06-01' and '2005-06-15'. Use the BETWEEN ... AND ... keywords.
rubric: Selected rental_id, rental_date, inventory_id, and customer_id
Named the correct table: rental
Used BETWEEN ... AND ... (not just > and <)
Dates written as 'YYYY-MM-DD' strings in the correct order (start, then end)
questions.explanation: BETWEEN...AND... is inclusive of both endpoints and reads more clearly than chaining >= and <=.

questions.question:
This professor's exam ERDs use a 'Connector Options' legend of six symbols (a line ending in different combinations of a circle, a bar, or a crow's foot) to mark cardinality/participation on each end of a relationship. Match each connector to what it represents.

A = line + crow's foot only (no bar, no circle)
B = line + single bar + crow's foot
C = line + circle + crow's foot
D = line + single bar only (no crow's foot)
E = line + double bar (no crow's foot)
F = line + circle + single bar (no crow's foot)

pairs.right: One or many (mandatory many / "at least one")
Zero or many (optional many)
One and only one (mandatory one)
Zero or one (optional one)
Not a valid cardinality/participation symbol — a crow's foot alone doesn't specify mandatory or optional
Not a valid cardinality/participation symbol — a single bar alone doesn't specify one or many

questions.explanation: Crow's Foot notation always pairs a cardinality mark (single line = one, crow's foot = many) with a participation mark (double bar = mandatory, circle = optional). A or D alone are incomplete/distractor symbols.

questions.question: On this professor's completed ERDs, an attribute name shown in bold and underlined represents the entity's:
questions.explanation: Primary key attributes are listed first and marked bold/underlined at the top of the entity box, above a dividing line.

questions.question: On this professor's completed ERDs, an attribute name shown in italics (below the dividing line) typically represents a ______ key.
questions.explanation: Foreign key attributes are conventionally italicized to distinguish them from the primary key and from plain descriptive attributes.

questions.question: Business rule: "A CUSTOMER can place many ORDERS, but each ORDER is placed by exactly one CUSTOMER." What is the cardinality between CUSTOMER and ORDER?
questions.explanation: One customer relates to many orders, while each order relates to only one customer — a classic 1:M relationship.

questions.question: In Crow's Foot notation, a relationship in which an entity does not have to participate (the minimum cardinality is zero) is called ______ participation.
questions.explanation: Optional participation (shown with a circle) means an entity instance doesn't need a related row on the other side; mandatory participation requires one.

questions.question: Using the Connector Options legend above, which letter represents "one and only one" (mandatory one)?
questions.explanation: Two parallel lines (a double bar) mean mandatory one. A circle adds "optional," and a crow's foot adds "many."

questions.question: On an ERD, where does the foreign key go for a 1:M relationship between CUSTOMER (1) and ORDER (M)?
options: In the CUSTOMER table, referencing ORDER's primary key
In the ORDER table, referencing CUSTOMER's primary key
Foreign keys aren't needed for 1:M relationships
questions.explanation: The foreign key always goes on the "many" side of a 1:M relationship, referencing the primary key on the "one" side.

questions.question: Business rule: "One PROFESSOR teaches many CLASSes, but a CLASS is taught by only one PROFESSOR." The foreign key PROFESSOR_ID would be placed in the ______ table.
questions.explanation: CLASS is on the "many" side of this 1:M relationship, so it holds PROFESSOR_ID as a foreign key.

questions.question: Business rules: "A DEPARTMENT must employ at least one EMPLOYEE, and can employ many. Every EMPLOYEE must work for exactly one DEPARTMENT." Looking from EMPLOYEE toward DEPARTMENT, which connector belongs on the DEPARTMENT end of the relationship line?
options: Connector E (double bar) — one and only one
Connector C (circle + crow's foot) — zero or many
Connector F (circle + bar) — zero or one
Connector B (bar + crow's foot) — one or many
questions.explanation: Each EMPLOYEE works for exactly one DEPARTMENT — mandatory, and a maximum of one — so the DEPARTMENT end gets connector E (mandatory one).

questions.question: Same business rules as above ("A DEPARTMENT must employ at least one EMPLOYEE, and can employ many"). Looking from DEPARTMENT toward EMPLOYEE, which connector belongs on the EMPLOYEE end?
options: Connector E (double bar) — one and only one
Connector F (circle + bar) — zero or one
Connector B (bar + crow's foot) — one or many
Connector C (circle + crow's foot) — zero or many
questions.explanation: A DEPARTMENT must have at least one EMPLOYEE (mandatory) and can have many, so the EMPLOYEE end gets connector B (mandatory many / one or many).

questions.question: Business rules: "A CUSTOMER may or may not have placed any ORDERS yet. A CUSTOMER can place many ORDERS. Every ORDER must be placed by exactly one CUSTOMER." Looking from CUSTOMER toward ORDER, which connector belongs on the ORDER end?
options: Connector E (double bar) — one and only one
Connector B (bar + crow's foot) — one or many
Connector C (circle + crow's foot) — zero or many
Connector F (circle + bar) — zero or one
questions.explanation: A CUSTOMER might have zero orders (optional) but could have many, so the ORDER end gets connector C (optional many). Compare this to the DEPARTMENT/EMPLOYEE example, where participation was mandatory instead.

questions.question: Business rule: STUDENTs can enroll in many CLASSes, and each CLASS can have many STUDENTs. How should this be modeled on the ERD?
options: Put a foreign key in the STUDENT table
Put a foreign key in the CLASS table
Create a composite/bridge entity holding both primary keys as foreign keys
Merge STUDENT and CLASS into one table
questions.explanation: M:N relationships require a bridge (associative) entity containing both related primary keys as foreign keys.

questions.question: In the STUDENT/CLASS example above, the resulting bridge entity (e.g. ENROLLMENT) would most likely use a ______ primary key made up of STUDENT_ID and CLASS_ID together.
questions.explanation: A bridge entity's primary key is typically a composite key formed from the two foreign keys it holds.

questions.question: On a completed ERD, an entity's primary key is typically shown:
options: Below a horizontal line inside the entity box
At the top of the attribute list, often bold and underlined, above a dividing line
It is never shown on an ERD
questions.explanation: Primary key attributes are conventionally listed first (and marked, e.g. bold/underlined) at the top of the entity box.

questions.question: An attribute in an entity box that is neither the primary key nor a foreign key (shown in plain text, not bold or italic) is simply called a ______ attribute.
questions.explanation: Descriptive (non-key) attributes describe the entity but don't participate in identifying rows or linking tables.

questions.question: A STUDENT table stores three separate columns — COURSE_ID_1, COURSE_ID_2, COURSE_ID_3 — to hold up to three courses a student is taking. This design contains a:
questions.explanation: Multiple entries of the same type (course IDs) repeated across columns for one key is a repeating group — the first thing eliminated when converting a table to 1NF.

questions.question: The three-step procedure to convert a table to first normal form is: eliminate the repeating groups, identify the primary key, and identify all ______.
questions.explanation: 1NF conversion: eliminate repeating groups, identify the primary key, then identify all dependencies (often shown in a dependency diagram).

questions.question: A table is in 1NF, has no partial dependencies, but one non-key attribute (STU_HRS) determines another non-key attribute (STU_CLASS). What's the highest normal form this table currently satisfies?
questions.explanation: No partial dependency means it clears 2NF, but a dependency between two non-key attributes is a transitive dependency, which violates 3NF.

questions.question:
An ASSIGNMENT table (1NF) has composite primary key (PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM) and attributes PROJ_NAME, EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR, and HOURS, where:
• PROJ_NUM determines PROJ_NAME
• EMP_NUM determines EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, and CHG_HOUR
• the full composite key determines HOURS

Write out the dependency set for this table, and label each dependency as partial or full.
questions.modelAnswer:
PROJ_NUM -> PROJ_NAME  (partial dependency)
EMP_NUM -> EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR  (partial dependency)
(PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM) -> HOURS  (full functional dependency on the composite key)
rubric: Listed PROJ_NUM -> PROJ_NAME and correctly labeled it partial
Listed EMP_NUM -> EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR and correctly labeled it partial
Listed (PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM) -> HOURS and correctly labeled it a full functional dependency
questions.explanation: A dependency is 'partial' when the determinant is only part of the composite key; it's 'full' when the whole composite key is required to determine the attribute.

questions.question: Using the dependency set above, decompose the ASSIGNMENT table into 2NF. List the resulting tables with their attributes, underlining each primary key.
questions.modelAnswer:
PROJECT(PROJ_NUM, PROJ_NAME)
EMPLOYEE(EMP_NUM, EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR)
ASSIGNMENT(PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM, HOURS)
rubric: Created a PROJECT table keyed on PROJ_NUM, holding PROJ_NAME
Created an EMPLOYEE table keyed on EMP_NUM, holding EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR
Kept a bridge ASSIGNMENT table with composite key (PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM) and HOURS
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependencies by moving each into its own table, keyed on its determinant, and keeping the composite-key fact (HOURS) in the original bridge table.

questions.question: In the 2NF EMPLOYEE table above, EMP_NUM determines JOB_CLASS, and JOB_CLASS determines CHG_HOUR. What kind of dependency is EMP_NUM -> CHG_HOUR?
questions.explanation: CHG_HOUR depends on EMP_NUM only indirectly, through JOB_CLASS — that's the definition of a transitive dependency.

questions.question: Continue the decomposition to 3NF by removing the transitive dependency identified above. List all resulting tables.
questions.modelAnswer:
EMPLOYEE(EMP_NUM, EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS)
JOB(JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR)
PROJECT(PROJ_NUM, PROJ_NAME)
ASSIGNMENT(PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM, HOURS)
rubric: Split JOB_CLASS/CHG_HOUR out into a new JOB table keyed on JOB_CLASS
EMPLOYEE table no longer includes CHG_HOUR directly
PROJECT and ASSIGNMENT tables carried over unchanged from the 2NF decomposition
questions.explanation: Splitting JOB_CLASS/CHG_HOUR into its own JOB table removes the transitive dependency, leaving every table in 3NF.

questions.question: Second normal form (2NF) requires eliminating transitive dependencies.
questions.explanation: Eliminating transitive dependencies is the requirement for 3NF. 2NF requires eliminating partial dependencies.

questions.question: A dependency in which a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (rather than directly on the primary key) is called a ______ dependency.
questions.explanation: Transitive dependencies are what 3NF eliminates.

questions.question: Which of these correctly summarizes the requirement for 3NF?
options: Every determinant is a candidate key
No repeating groups exist anywhere in the database
questions.explanation: 3NF builds on 2NF by additionally requiring the elimination of transitive dependencies.

questions.question: Denormalization is done to reduce data redundancy at the cost of processing speed.
questions.explanation: It's the opposite: denormalization increases redundancy but can improve processing speed by reducing the number of joins needed.

questions.question: More tables generally require more join operations to reconstruct a full picture of the data. This is the main tradeoff of:
options: Normalization increasing the number of tables
questions.explanation: Normalization reduces redundancy but increases the number of tables, which means more I/O operations and processing logic to join them back together.
